3. On behalf of the respondents affidavit-in--opposition has been filed stating, inter alia, that after publication of the result of BA (Pass) Examination of 1987 respondent No. 3 received a complaint on 11.8.88 that various persons including the petitioner illegally attached the answer scripts in Islamic History and Culture and of Philosophy some additional answers to some more questions written from outside the examination hall. The answer scripts of the petitioner and 4 others of Barhamganj College were collected carefully scrutinized and was found to be true. A corrigendum was issued by respondent No. 3 on 14.9.88 deleting the result of the petitioner and 4 others from the provisional result sheet dated 23.7.88 and the publication of the result of the petitioner and 4 others were withheld for a final decision of the Discipline Board and the Syndicate of the Dhaka University. The petitioner appeared before the Assistant Controller of Examination on 27.11.88. A specimen hand writing of the petitioner was collected by the said Assistant Controller-2 through dictation. The Respondents found that the writings of these illegally attached answers were quite different from the other answers of the scripts and that the pen and the ink used in writing the illegally attached pages were also different from those of the other answer scripts. The respondents found that the allegations brought against the petitioner were sufficiently proved. The respondents took some time to collect all the examination records of the petitioner. His case was carefully examined by the Discipline Board of the University. The Discipline Board in its meeting held on 12.11.89 considered the allegations against the petitioner and the reply submitted by the petitioner and also considered the handwriting of all other papers and found the petitioner guilty of the aforesaid examination offence as defined in Chapter XLII of the Dhaka University Ordinances and Regulations and recommended imposition of penalty by cancellation of the examination in question i.e. BA (Pass) Examination held in October/November, 1987 and debarred the petitioner from appearing in 3 subsequent examinations of the University. The Syndicate of the Dhaka University in its meeting on 28.11.89 approved the punishment recommended by Discipline Board against the petitioner and the said decision of the Syndicate was communicated to the Principal of Barhamganj College on 23.11.89. Therefore the question of issuance of marks certificate and provisional certificate to the petitioner does not arise as the petitioner never passed BA (Pass) Examination of 1987. The relationship of the student and the University being fiduciary the evaluation of academic attainment of a student is the sole function of the University in accordance with the Rules and Regulations of the University. As the decision taken by the University Authority against the petitioner is just and proper and in accordance with law, the writ petition filed by the petitioner is not maintainable. 

 5. Mr. Shafique Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the respondents, submitted that the University Authority followed all the relevant Rules and Regulations in respect of examination offences with reference to offence committed by the petitioner and duly and legally found the petitioner guilty and awarded punishment as considered to be necessary. He also submitted that in exercising the writ jurisdiction this Court generally speaking will not enter into the questions of fact and will confine itself to the question of legality of the matter and that as the petitioner has totally failed to show that the University Authority has committed any illegality, no interference by this Court is called for. He referred to the decision in the case of Wasim Ahmed Khan Vs. Secretary, Board of High School and Intermediate Education, UP Allahabad and another, AIR 1961 Allahabad 290 and Karamjit Kaur Vs. The Punjab University, AIR 1964 Punjab 327. In the case of Wasim Ahmed, AIR 1961 Allahabad 290 it was held that the question whether there had been copying or not is a pure question of fact in which the High Court in writ jurisdiction cannot interfere. It was also held that the question of malafides have to be proved and the High Court in writ jurisdiction will again not enter into such disputed fact of malafide. In the instant case the petitioner was given the opportunity to show cause and the petitioner has not been able to show that any illegality was committed in not following any Rule or Regulation. The University Authority duly examined the question as to whether the sheets were subsequently attached to the answer scripts in question and were written in different hand, in different ink and by different pen and taking into consideration the written submissions made by the petitioner came to the finding that in his aforesaid answer scripts the said offence had been committed, this Court in exercise of its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution will not enter into the question as to whether the University Authority came to a correct finding as this Court is not an Appellate Authority. In the case of Board of High School and Intermediate Education, UP Allahabad Vs. Bagleshwar Prasad, 1963 All Li 676 (SC), it was observed by the Indian Supreme Court: 

 "In dealing with petitions of this type, it is necessary to bear in mind that educational institutions like the Universities or appellant No. 1 set up Enquiry Committees to deal with the problem posed by the adoption of unfair means by candidates, and normally it is within the jurisdiction of such domestic Tribunals to decide all relevant questions in the light of the evidence adduced before them. In the matter of the adoption of unfair means, direct evidence may sometimes be available, but cases may arise where direct evidence is not available and the question will have to be considered in the light of probabilities and circumstantial evidence. This problem which educational institutions have to face from time to time is a serious problem and unless there is justification to do so, courts should be slow to interfere with the decisions of domestic Tribunals appointed by educational bodies like the Universities. In dealing with the validity of the impugned orders passed by Universities under Article 226 (writ jurisdiction of the Indian Constitution) the High Court is not sitting in appeal over the decision in question; its jurisdiction is limited and though it is true that if the impugned order is not supported by any evidence at all, the High Court would be justified to quash that order. But the conclusion that the impugned order is supported by any evidence must be reached after considering the question as to whether probabilities and circumstantial evidence do not justify the said conclusion. Enquiries held by domestic Tribunals in such cases must, no doubt, be fair and students against whom charges are framed must be given adequate opportunities to defend themselves, and in holding such enquiries, the Tribunals must scrupulously follow rules of natural justice; but it would, we think, not be reasonable to import into these enquiries all considerations which govern criminal trials in ordinary courts of law.
